Discovery of Hidden Miscalibration Regimes

Katarzyna Kobalczyk Affiliation: University of Cambridge Email: knk25@cam.ac.uk    Mihaela van der Schaar Affiliation: University of Cambridge Email: mv472@cam.ac.uk
Abstract

Calibration is commonly evaluated by comparing model confidence with its empirical correctness, implicitly treating reliability as a function of the confidence score alone. However, this view can hide substantial structure: models may be systematically overconfident on some kinds of inputs and underconfident on others, causing global reliability diagnostics to obscure localised calibration failures. To address this, we formulate the problem of discovering hidden miscalibration regimes without assuming access to predefined data slices. We define the corresponding miscalibration field and propose a diagnostic framework for estimating it. Our approach learns a calibration-aware representation of the input space and estimates signed local miscalibration by kernel smoothing in the learned geometry. Across four real-world LLM benchmarks and twelve LLMs, we find that input-dependent calibration heterogeneity is prevalent. We further show that the discovered fields are actionable: they support local confidence correction and reduce calibration error in systematically miscalibrated regions where confidence-based methods such as isotonic regression and temperature scaling are less effective.

1 Introduction

Can calibration failures have hidden structure?

Calibration is usually evaluated by comparing a model’s reported confidence with empirical correctness. A classifier that predicts 70%70\% confidence should be correct roughly 70%70\% of the time, and reliability diagrams operationalise this idea by grouping predictions according to their confidence scores (Guo et al., 2017). This view is simple and widely used, but it makes a strong aggregation assumption: reliability is treated as a function of the confidence score alone. All inputs assigned the same confidence are implicitly treated as exchangeable for the purpose of calibration analysis, regardless of what those inputs are.

This assumption can fail in heterogeneous domains. A model may be systematically overconfident on one kind of input and underconfident on another, even when both kinds of inputs receive similar confidence scores. In that case, global reliability diagrams can hide rather than reveal calibration failures: opposing errors cancel when aggregated by confidence. Slice-based analysis (Hebert-Johnson et al., 2018) can expose such failures when the relevant groups are known in advance, but in complex domains the miscalibrated regions need not align with available metadata, dataset labels, or obvious human-defined partitions. This issue may be especially relevant for large language models (LLMs), which are trained on broad corpora and deployed across tasks that vary in semantics, difficulty, format, and ambiguity.

Discovering hidden miscalibration regimes.

We therefore study calibration as an input-dependent discovery problem. Without access to predefined data slices or ground-truth data-generating probabilities, can we recover regions of the input space where the model is systematically overconfident or underconfident? Our central premise is that calibration failures often follow latent structure: inputs that are similar in meaning, context, or task type may exhibit similar calibration trends. If this structure can be revealed, we can identify hidden calibration regimes, quantify how much miscalibration is obscured by global diagnostics, and analyse how reliability varies across tasks or semantic domains.

Learning a miscalibration field.

To formalise this discovery problem, we define an input-dependent miscalibration field. Unlike reliability diagrams, which condition on scalar confidence scores, this field measures signed calibration error over the input space itself. We estimate this field by learning a representation in which examples with similar calibration behaviour are close together. In this learned geometry, local averaging of residuals reveals coherent regions of over- and underconfidence. The resulting estimator is primarily a diagnostic object: it identifies where calibration errors occur, their direction, and how strongly they vary across the input space. The same field can also be used downstream for local confidence correction.

Calibration heterogeneity in modern LLMs.

We first validate the framework on controlled synthetic experiments where the true miscalibration structure is known. We then use it as a diagnostic tool in a large-scale study of LLM predictions across four real-world benchmarks and twelve base models from different families. The synthetic experiments show that the method recovers known hidden miscalibration structure from noisy residuals. On LLM benchmarks, we find that input-dependent calibration heterogeneity appears across many settings but is not uniform: some model–dataset pairs exhibit mostly homogeneous bias, while others contain pronounced hidden regimes of overconfidence and underconfidence. Moreover, the degree of heterogeneity predicts when local correction is most useful: in highly heterogeneous settings, the learned field reduces slice-level calibration error where confidence-based post-hoc methods can remain unreliable.

Contributions.

▶\blacktriangleright Hidden regime discovery. We formulate the problem of discovering coherent regions of over- and underconfidence without predefined slices or subgroup labels. ▶\blacktriangleright Miscalibration fields. We define an input-dependent miscalibration field that captures where signed calibration error varies across the input space, rather than only as a function of confidence. ▶\blacktriangleright Calibration-aware geometry. We introduce a diagnostic framework that learns a representation in which local residual averaging exposes stable regime-level calibration structure. ▶\blacktriangleright LLM evidence. Across four benchmarks and twelve LLMs, we show that calibration heterogeneity is present but non-uniform, varying across datasets, model families, and scales. ▶\blacktriangleright Actionable local correction. The learned field supports targeted confidence correction, reducing calibration error in high-error regions where confidence-based post-hoc methods are less effective.

2 Background, Related Work, and Problem Setup

In this section we introduce the notation and background, focusing on the notions most directly relevant to our setting; an extended discussion of related work is provided in Appendix A.

The Classical View: Calibration in the Confidence Space.

Consider a binary classifier that assigns each input x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} a confidence score f⁡(x)∈[0,1]f(x)\in[0,1], interpreted as an estimate of the conditional probability η⁡(x)=ℙ⁡(Y=1∣X=x)=𝔼⁡[Y∣X=x]\eta(x)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid X=x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x], where Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\}. Classical calibration asks whether predictions assigned a given confidence are correct at the corresponding frequency (Dawid, 1982; DeGroot and Fienberg, 1983). Formally, the calibration function is μ⁡(f)=𝔼⁡[Y∣f⁡(X)=f]\mu(f)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid f(X)=f], and a model is perfectly calibrated if μ⁡(f)=f\mu(f)=f for all confidence values ff. Equivalently, defining the residual R=Y−f⁡(X)R=Y-f(X), score-conditioned miscalibration can be written as δ⁡(f)=𝔼⁡[R∣f⁡(X)=f]\delta(f)=\mathbb{E}[R\mid f(X)=f]. Positive or negative values indicate underconfidence or overconfidence, respectively.

In practice, μ⁡(f)\mu(f) and δ⁡(f)\delta(f) are estimated by grouping examples with similar confidence scores. Reliability diagrams approximate the calibration curve by binning predictions according to f⁡(x)f(x) and comparing average confidence with empirical accuracy within each bin (DeGroot and Fienberg, 1983; Guo et al., 2017). The expected calibration error (ECE) summarises the magnitude of these binned deviations and is widely used in modern neural-network calibration studies (Guo et al., 2017). A smooth alternative replaces hard binning with kernel smoothing in the confidence space, yielding a smoothed reliability diagram (Blasiok and Nakkiran, 2024) with its corresponding version of the ECE, SmoothECE (smECE). As we will see, our method generalises this idea: instead of smoothing residuals among examples with similar confidence scores, we smooth residuals among examples that are close in a learned input representation.

Post-hoc calibration methods such as Platt scaling (Platt, 1999), temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017), and isotonic regression (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2001; Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002) also operate in the confidence space: they learn a mapping from the scalar score f⁡(x)f(x) to a calibrated probability. This confidence-based perspective is widely adopted, but it makes an important aggregation choice: calibration is studied as a function of the score f⁡(x)f(x) alone. All inputs assigned similar confidence values are treated as exchangeable for the purpose of calibration analysis, regardless of where they lie in the input space.

Hidden Regimes.

In heterogeneous datasets, the same confidence value may correspond to different calibration behaviour depending on the type of the input xx. A model may be systematically overconfident on one type of inputs and underconfident on others. When calibration is evaluated only as a function of confidence, these effects can cancel, producing reliability diagrams that appear well calibrated even though substantial local miscalibration remains. Figure 1 illustrates this failure mode: aggregation by confidence scores alone hides distinct regions of overconfidence and underconfidence.

A standard way to diagnose input-dependent calibration is slice-based analysis, where reliability is evaluated separately within predefined subgroups. This is closely related to subgroup calibration and multicalibration, which require calibration to hold across a collection of subpopulations (Hebert-Johnson et al., 2018). However, these approaches require the relevant slices or subgroup classes to be specified in advance. In high-dimensional domains such as language and vision, the regions where miscalibration occurs may not align with dataset labels or any obvious human-defined partition. This motivates an automatic approach: instead of asking whether a model is calibrated on predefined groups, we aim to discover and quantify miscalibration heterogeneity directly from observed predictions and outcomes.

Our Object of Study: The Miscalibration Field.

We are given i.i.d. triples (xi,fi,yi)(x_{i},f_{i},y_{i}), where xi∈𝒳x_{i}\in\mathcal{X}, fi=f⁡(xi)∈[0,1]f_{i}=f(x_{i})\in[0,1], and yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\}. Our goal is to discover regions of the input space where the model is systematically overconfident or underconfident without assuming access to predefined data slices.

To formalise this goal, we define the input-dependent miscalibration field as

δ⁡(x)=𝔼⁡[Y−f⁡(X)∣X=x]=𝔼⁡[R∣X=x].\delta(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y-f(X)\mid X=x]=\mathbb{E}[R\mid X=x]. (1)

Since δ⁡(x)=η⁡(x)−f⁡(x)\delta(x)=\eta(x)-f(x), the field measures the local difference between the model’s confidence and the true conditional probability. Thus δ⁡(x)<0\delta(x)<0 indicates local overconfidence and δ⁡(x)>0\delta(x)>0 indicates local underconfidence.

This differs from classical calibration, which studies 𝔼⁡[R∣f⁡(X)=f]\mathbb{E}[R\mid f(X)=f], a score-conditioned average over all inputs with the same confidence. This distinction is key: two inputs can have the same value of f⁡(x)f(x) while having different signs or magnitudes of δ⁡(x)\delta(x).Therefore, our objective is not to recalibrate confidence scores globally, but to recover input-space structure indicating where and in what direction calibration fails.

3 A Diagnostic Framework for Revealing Calibration Regimes

We now describe our procedure to estimate the input-dependent miscalibration field introduced in Section 2. Our goal is to learn a representation in which examples with similar calibration behaviour are organised close together. In such a geometry, local averaging of residuals provides stable estimates of systematic overconfidence and underconfidence.

3.1 Kernel Estimation in a Learned Representation

Let ri:=yi−fir_{i}:=y_{i}-f_{i} denote the empirical residual of example ii. Confidence-based smoothed calibration (Blasiok and Nakkiran, 2024) estimates score-conditioned residuals by averaging rir_{i} among examples with similar confidence values. We instead average residuals among examples that are close in a learned representation of the input. Let ϕ:𝒳→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a learnable representation map. Given a kernel bandwidth σ>0\sigma>0, define

Kσ​(ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(x′)):=exp⁡(−‖ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(x′)‖2σ2).K_{\sigma}(\phi(x),\phi(x^{\prime})):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\phi(x)-\phi(x^{\prime})\|^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right).

For a query point xx, we estimate δ⁡(x)\delta(x) by kernel smoothing the residuals in ϕ⁡(𝒳)\phi(\mathcal{X}):

δ^ϕ​(x)=∑i=1nKσ​(ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(xi))​ri∑i=1nKσ​(ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(xi)).\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{\sigma}(\phi(x),\phi(x_{i}))\,r_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{\sigma}(\phi(x),\phi(x_{i}))}. (2)

This is a Nadaraya–Watson (Nadaraya, 1964; Watson, 1964) estimator of 𝔼⁡[R∣ϕ⁡(X)=ϕ⁡(x)]\mathbb{E}[R\mid\phi(X)=\phi(x)], and therefore estimates a representation-smoothed version of the miscalibration field δ⁡(x)=𝔼⁡[R∣X=x]\delta(x)=\mathbb{E}[R\mid X=x]. The role of ϕ\phi is to induce a geometry in which this smoothed field remains informative, with nearby examples sharing homogeneous calibration behaviour.

Note, kernel estimates for validation and test points are computed using the training set as the neighbour bank. This ensures that evaluation does not use labels from the validation or test split to construct local neighbourhoods.

3.2 Learning Representations that Reveal Systematic Residuals

A useful representation should make systematic residual structure visible under local averaging. If ϕ\phi mixes examples with both positive and negative values of δ⁡(x)\delta(x) within the same neighbourhood, the empirical residuals tend to cancel resulting in δ^ϕ​(x)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) close to zero. Conversely, if ϕ\phi separates regions with distinct calibration behaviour, local residual averages have large magnitude and their sign reveals the corresponding over- and underconfident regimes.

This observation motivates learning ϕ\phi to maximise the variability of the conditional mean residual, Var⁡(𝔼⁡[R∣ϕ⁡(X)])\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[R\mid\phi(X)]). Since 𝔼⁡[R]\mathbb{E}[R] is independent of ϕ\phi, this is equivalent, up to an additive constant, to maximising the second moment 𝔼⁡[(𝔼⁡[R∣ϕ⁡(X)])2]\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[R\mid\phi(X)])^{2}]. We approximate this objective empirically by replacing 𝔼⁡[R∣ϕ⁡(X)=ϕ⁡(xi)]\mathbb{E}[R\mid\phi(X)=\phi(x_{i})] with the kernel estimate δ^ϕ​(xi)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x_{i}), yielding:

J^​(ϕ)=1n​∑i=1nδ^ϕ​(xi)2.\widehat{J}(\phi)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x_{i})^{2}. (3)

Maximizing Eq. (3) encourages representations in which local residual averages are non-cancelling and therefore expose systematic overconfidence and underconfidence in the input space.

Preventing Neighbourhood Collapse.

We note that the objective in Eq. (3) admits a degenerate solution: the representation can isolate each training point, making δ^ϕ​(xi)≈ri\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x_{i})\approx r_{i} and artificially increasing the objective by fitting Bernoulli noise. To prevent this, we regularise the effective neighbourhood mass mi:=∑j=1nKσ​(ϕ⁡(xi),ϕ⁡(xj))m_{i}:=\sum_{j=1}^{n}K_{\sigma}(\phi(x_{i}),\phi(x_{j})). Our final loss for training ϕ\phi is:

ℒ(ϕ)=−1n∑i=1nδ^ϕ(xi)2+λ1n∑i=1n[max(0,mmin−mi)]2,\mathcal{L}(\phi)=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x_{i})^{2}+\lambda\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\max(0,m_{\min}-m_{i})\right]^{2}, (4)

where mmin>0m_{\min}>0 is a target minimum neighbourhood mass and λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 controls the strength of the regularisation. The first term encourages discovery of systematic residual structure, while the second discourages isolated neighbourhoods and stabilises the estimator.

Hyperparameter Selection.

The training objective in Eq. (4) depends on the kernel bandwidth σ\sigma and the regularisation parameters mminm_{\min} and λ\lambda. As a result, losses are not directly comparable across hyperparameter settings. Moreover, in real applications the ground-truth miscalibration field δ⁡(x)\delta(x) is unknown, so oracle metrics such as Corr⁡(δ^ϕ​(X),δ⁡(X))\mathrm{Corr}(\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(X),\delta(X)) cannot be used for model selection. To address this, we use a validation proxy based only on the observed triples (xi,fi,yi)(x_{i},f_{i},y_{i}). Specifically, for a candidate representation ϕ\phi we compute locally corrected predictions as f​(x)+δ^ϕ​(x)f(x)+\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) on the validation split and evaluate the resulting Brier score. Hyperparameters are selected to minimise this corrected validation Brier score. This additive criterion is aligned with the fact that δ⁡(x)\delta(x) is a conditional mean residual: under squared loss, the optimal probability correction is precisely the conditional mean of Y−f⁡(X)Y-f(X). A detailed description of the proxy is provided in Appendix B.

3.3 Intuition: Variance Reduction by Local Averaging

Estimating δ⁡(x)\delta(x) is difficult because individual residuals are noisy. Under the standard model Y|X=x∼Bernoulli⁡(η⁡(x))Y\mid X=x\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\eta(x)), residuals R=Y−f⁡(X)R=Y-f(X) satisfy 𝔼⁡[R∣X=x]=δ⁡(x)\mathbb{E}[R\mid X=x]=\delta(x) and have conditional variance Var⁡(R∣X=x)=η⁡(x)​(1−η⁡(x))\mathrm{Var}(R\mid X=x)=\eta(x)(1-\eta(x)). Thus, when η⁡(x)\eta(x) is not close to 00 or 11, each residual is a high-variance observation whose conditional mean is the local miscalibration field δ⁡(x)\delta(x). Kernel smoothing reduces this variance by averaging residuals over local neighbourhoods. The following result formalises this variance-reduction effect for a fixed representation:

While this result is not a recovery guarantee for the learned geometry, it explains the variance-reduction mechanism of local averaging once ϕ\phi is fixed. It also motivates the neighbourhood-mass regulariser in Eq. (4): isolated points lead to high-variance residual estimates; sufficiently large neighbourhoods provide stable local averages. This contrasts with the alternative possibility of direct residual regression, which attempts to learn a pointwise mapping from high-variance Bernoulli residuals (see Appendix E.6 for an empirical comparison).

3.4 Actionable Use of the Learned Field: Local Recalibration

The learned field δ^ϕ​(x)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) is primarily a diagnostic object: it identifies where the model is locally overconfident or underconfident. However, it can also be used downstream to correct model confidences.

A naive additive correction f​(x)+δ^ϕ​(x)f(x)+\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) may fall outside the valid probability range. For a confidence score f⁡(x)f(x), any valid additive correction must lie in [−f⁡(x),1−f⁡(x)][-f(x),1-f(x)]. We therefore use a range-aware correction map that preserves the sign of δ^ϕ​(x)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) and is monotone in its magnitude, while smoothly saturating at the feasible endpoints. For a scale parameter α>0\alpha>0, define

Δα​(x)={−f⁡(x)​tanh⁡(α​|δ^ϕ​(x)|),δ^ϕ​(x)<0,(1−f⁡(x))​tanh⁡(α​|δ^ϕ​(x)|),δ^ϕ​(x)≥0.\Delta_{\alpha}(x)=\begin{cases}-f(x)\tanh\!\left(\alpha|\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)|\right),&\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)<0,\\[4.0pt] (1-f(x))\tanh\!\left(\alpha|\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)|\right),&\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)\geq 0.\end{cases}

The corrected confidence is then

f~​(x)=f⁡(x)+Δα​(x).\tilde{f}(x)=f(x)+\Delta_{\alpha}(x). (5)

This guarantees f~​(x)∈[0,1]\tilde{f}(x)\in[0,1] without hard clipping. The scalar α\alpha is selected on the validation split after the representation map ϕ\phi has been fixed. Thus, learning the field and converting it into final probabilities are separated: the representation is selected to reveal local calibration structure, while the range-aware map provides a post-hoc correction of the probabilistic predictions.

In the next section, we evaluate the proposed framework through two complementary sets of experiments: controlled synthetic datasets that allow us to study recovery of known miscalibration structures (Section 4), and real-world experiments on large language model predictions that demonstrate the presence of input-dependent calibration heterogeneity in practice (Section 5).

4 Experiments: Synthetic Illustrations

We first use controlled synthetic experiments to validate three aspects of the proposed estimator: (i) it can uncover hidden calibration regimes that are invisible to score-based diagnostics, (ii) it can recover smoothly varying miscalibration fields from noisy Bernoulli residuals, and (iii) its hyperparameters can be selected without oracle access to the true field δ⁡(x)\delta(x). Full data-generating details and additional studies are provided in Appendix E.

Setup.

We generate two datasets: three-cluster and sinusoidal, each with n=10,000n=10{,}000 samples constructed as triples (xi,fi,yi)(x_{i},f_{i},y_{i}), with xi∈ℝ2x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. Datasets are split into train/validation/test sets with proportions 80/10/1080/10/10. The representation map ϕ\phi is implemented as a two-layer MLP. At validation and test time, δ^ϕ​(x)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) is estimated by kernel smoothing in the learned representation space using the training set as the neighbour bank. Since δ⁡(x)\delta(x) is known in these controlled settings, we evaluate recovery using the Pearson correlation between δ^ϕ​(X)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(X) and δ⁡(X)\delta(X) on the test set.

Hidden clustered regimes.

In the three-cluster dataset, model confidence f⁡(x)f(x) is generated from a base logit function ℓ⁡(x)\ell(x), while the true conditional probability includes a cluster-dependent shift. Specifically, for a point xx in cluster c⁡(x)c(x), we set f⁡(x)=sigm⁡(ℓ⁡(x))f(x)=\mathrm{sigm}(\ell(x)) and η⁡(x)=sigm⁡(ℓ⁡(x)+Δc⁡(x))\eta(x)=\mathrm{sigm}(\ell(x)+\Delta_{c(x)}), with Δc∈{−1,0,+1}\Delta_{c}\in\{-1,0,+1\}. Labels are then sampled from Bernoulli⁡(η⁡(x))\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\eta(x)), defining the ground-truth miscalibration field as δ⁡(x)=η⁡(x)−f⁡(x)\delta(x)=\eta(x)-f(x). This construction induces piecewise-structured miscalibration in the input space (Fig. 2a, left). As shown in Fig. 2b, the global reliability diagram suggests near calibration because opposing errors cancel when examples are aggregated by confidence alone. However, the cluster-level reliability diagrams reveal substantial systematic miscalibration. The learned field δ^ϕ​(x)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) recovers this hidden structure from (x,f,y)(x,f,y) alone, without access to η⁡(x)\eta(x) or cluster labels, achieving test correlation r=0.95r=0.95 with the true field (Fig. 2a, right).

Smooth miscalibration fields.

We next replace the discrete cluster shifts with a smooth input-dependent logit shift. As before, the model confidence is f⁡(x)=sigm⁡(ℓ⁡(x))f(x)=\mathrm{sigm}(\ell(x)), but the true conditional probability is η⁡(x)=sigm⁡(ℓ⁡(x)+Δ⁡(x))\eta(x)=\mathrm{sigm}(\ell(x)+\Delta(x)), where Δ⁡(x)=A​sin⁡(2​π​k​u⊤​x)\Delta(x)=A\sin(2\pi ku^{\top}x). Here uu is a fixed unit direction, AA controls the strength of miscalibration, and kk controls the spatial frequency of regime alternation. This induces a continuously varying ground-truth field δ⁡(x)=η⁡(x)−f⁡(x)\delta(x)=\eta(x)-f(x) (see Appendix E.3 for a visualization) and tests whether the method can recover input-dependent miscalibration beyond discrete clusters. Fig. 2c shows that the learned estimator captures the sign and spatial structure of the true field. Across amplitudes and frequencies, recovery remains strong and degrades mainly when the field is both weak and rapidly oscillating, that is when the signal-to-noise ratio of the residuals is lowest.

Proxy-based hyperparameter selection.

The previous evaluations use the known field δ⁡(x)\delta(x) only for reporting test recovery. In practice, however, δ⁡(x)\delta(x) is unobserved, so hyperparameters such as the bandwidth σ\sigma and mass-regularisation strength λ\lambda must be chosen from the observed triples (xi,fi,yi)(x_{i},f_{i},y_{i}) alone. In this experiment, we evaluate the validation proxy introduced in Section 3.2. For each sinusoidal setting, specified by a signal strength AA and frequency kk, we evaluate a grid of hyperparameters (σ,λ)(\sigma,\lambda) and compare the proxy-selected choice (σ^,λ^)(\hat{\sigma},\hat{\lambda}) against the oracle objective O⁡(σ,λ)=Corr⁡(δ^ϕ​(X),δ⁡(X))O(\sigma,\lambda)=\mathrm{Corr}(\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(X),\delta(X)) computed on the test set. We summarise each setting by three quantities: 1) the Spearman rank correlation between the negated validation proxy and O⁡(σ,λ)O(\sigma,\lambda) across the grid, so that larger Spearman rank values indicate better rank agreement; 2) the oracle spread Δ​O=Omax−Omin\Delta O=O_{\max}-O_{\min}, which measures how much performance varies over the grid; 3) the selection regret O∗−O⁡(σ^,λ^)O^{*}-O(\hat{\sigma},\hat{\lambda}), where O∗=maxσ,λ⁡O⁡(σ,λ)O^{*}=\max_{\sigma,\lambda}O(\sigma,\lambda). Each point in Fig. 3 corresponds to one sinusoidal setting (A,k)(A,k). The left panel shows that stronger proxy–oracle rank agreement is associated with lower regret. The right panel shows how rank agreement varies with oracle spread: when the oracle surface is flat, rankings are less stable because many hyperparameter choices have similar oracle performance. Overall, proxy selection achieves low regret in most settings, with median regret of just 0.0080.008; the full regret table by (A,k)(A,k) is given in Appendix E.5.

Additional experiments.

Appendix E provides full synthetic details and extended results: the complete data-generating processes, sensitivity to bandwidth σ\sigma and mass regularisation λ\lambda, extended proxy-selection diagnostics, and a comparison with direct residual regression, which is demonstrated to be less stable in low-signal or high-frequency regimes.

5 Experiments: Discovering Hidden Calibration Regimes of Modern LLMs

We next investigate whether input-dependent calibration heterogeneity arises in real-world language model predictions. We evaluate four datasets: HH-RLHF (Bai et al., 2022), MedMCQA (Pal et al., 2022), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), and MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024); and four model families: Qwen-3, Ministral-3, Llama-3.1/2, and Gemma-3; across varying model sizes (12 LLMs in total). We focus on base LLMs—prior work suggests that post-training and alignment can degrade calibration, while base models often remain better calibrated (Zhu et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2025; Nakkiran et al., 2026). Compared with instruction- and RL-tuned models, base LLMs tend to produce confidence scores spanning a broader range of values in [0,1][0,1], making them a natural setting for visualising and studying input-dependent calibration heterogeneity. For each dataset–model pair, we learn the representation map ϕ\phi on the training split, select hyperparameters on the validation split using our proxy defined in Section 3.2, and report all results on the test split, using the training points as the neighbour bank.

We organize the results around three axes: discovery, whether the learned field identifies hidden high-error regimes; validity, whether these regimes are meaningful and stable; and actionability, whether the discovered structure can be used for local correction.

A representative example.

We start with a representative example of the HH-RLHF dataset on Qwen3-8B. HH-RLHF consists of prompts paired with two candidate responses and a human preference label. We treat the model’s predicted preference probability for the first response as the confidence score f⁡(x)f(x), and define y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} to indicate whether the first response is preferred by the human annotator (response order is sampled randomly).

Figure 4 shows reliability diagrams for the full test set, the original HH-RLHF helpful/harmless slices, and the regions discovered by the learned miscalibration field defined as: overconfident {x:δ^ϕ​(x)<−ϵ}\{x:\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)<-\epsilon\} and underconfident {x:δ^ϕ​(x)>ϵ}\{x:\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)>\epsilon\}, where we set ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05. Although the aggregate reliability diagram suggests only moderate miscalibration, conditioning on δ^ϕ\widehat{\delta}_{\phi} reveals substantially stronger and opposing calibration errors. Importantly, this example shows that inputs with similar confidence values can belong to different calibration regimes, and therefore that calibration cannot be fully characterised as a function of the scalar confidence score alone.

Discovery: the learned field identifies hidden calibration regimes.

We next characterise the learned miscalibration fields across all 48 dataset–model pairs included in this study. Figure 5 separates two properties of the field: its mean, which captures the overall calibration bias, and its standard deviation, which captures input-dependent heterogeneity. The structure of the learned fields varies. Some settings exhibit mostly homogeneous overconfidence, while others display high calibration heterogeneity (e.g. Qwen-3 on HH-RLHF, Llama-3.1/2 on MMLU). Appendix F.1 shows the same figure with points annotated by exact model sizes.

Importantly, this learned variability is meaningful. Figure 5b reports the gap between the worst-slice and global smECE on the test sets, with slices defined by δ^ϕ\hat{\delta}_{\phi}, as previously. We define the worst slice as the higher-smECE region among the discovered overconfident and underconfident slices. Large values indicate that the aggregate reliability metrics substantially underestimate calibration error in some region of the input space. Thus, the learned field identifies regions with genuinely worse calibration.

Validity: the discovered regimes are stable.

The discovered regimes are not rare edge cases. Among the 18 dataset–model pairs with a worst-slice smECE gap of at least 0.060.06, the worst-calibrated slice contains on average 41%41\% of test examples. Additional analyses support the reliability of these regimes: Appendix F.3 reruns the full pipeline under label permutation and across random seeds. Appendix F.5 reports bootstrap confidence intervals for worst-slice gaps and slice sizes, while Appendix F.4 shows robustness across thresholds. Finally, Appendix F.2 shows that raw hidden-state smoothing mostly recovers global overconfidence, rather than signed hidden regimes.

Actionability: local correction.

The learned field can also be used to locally correct model confidence as introduced in Section 3.4. We use two confidence-based calibrators as controls for whether the discovered structure can be explained by the scalar confidence alone: isotonic regression (ISO) and temperature scaling (TS). Figure 6 reports the absolute improvement in smECE relative to the raw model, aggregated across all 12 LLMs. Confidence-based methods improve global calibration (all data), but their behaviour is less consistent across the discovered regimes and often degrades calibration on the already well-calibrated subsets. In contrast, our method consistently reduces calibration error in the over- and underconfident regions while preserving performance on the well-calibrated subset. This demonstrates that the learned field is not only diagnostic, but also actionable: it enables local corrections that cannot be achieved from confidence scores alone.

When does local calibration help?

We also examine when input-dependent calibration provides the largest advantage. Figure 7a shows that the benefit of our method over ISO on the worst-calibrated slice increases with the standard deviation of the learned miscalibration field. This relationship supports the central claim of the paper: local calibration is most useful when calibration behaviour varies substantially across inputs.

What is the effect of model size?

Finally, we study how heterogeneity varies with model scale. As shown in Figure 7b, in several model families, calibration heterogeneity increases with model size. One possible explanation is that model capabilities improve non-uniformly across domains as scale increases, producing regions where confidence becomes better aligned with correctness and others where systematic miscalibration persists or becomes amplified.

6 Discussion

We formulated the problem of discovering hidden calibration regimes: regions of coherent over- or underconfidence that can be obscured by confidence-based diagnostics. To study this failure mode, we define a miscalibration field over the input space and estimate it by learning a calibration-aware geometry in which local averaging of residuals reveals coherent regime-level structure. Synthetic experiments validate recovery of known miscalibration fields, while LLM experiments show substantial input-dependent calibration heterogeneity across datasets and model families.

The proposed estimator should be viewed as a diagnostic instrument rather than a complete solution to local calibration. Its purpose is to reveal signed residual structure and to test whether the learned field is actionable. The local recalibration results illustrate that the discovered regimes can support targeted confidence correction beyond confidence-only transformations, while richer input-dependent calibrators remain an important complementary direction. The current formulation focuses on binary correctness, leaving multiclass settings and open-ended generation for future work. Finally, the learned geometry provides a starting point for interpretability (see Appendix F.6): although this work does not explain why a regime is miscalibrated, the representation can be inspected using metadata or semantic descriptors opening a path toward interpretable calibration debugging.

Overall, our results suggest that calibration should not be viewed only as a global property of confidence scores. Discovering hidden over- and underconfident regions is an important step toward more reliable uncertainty estimates for models deployed across heterogeneous tasks and domains.

Appendix A Extended Related Work

Our work sits at the intersection of calibration, subgroup reliability, and automatic slice discovery, but differs from each in its object of study. Standard post-hoc calibration methods estimate reliability as a function of the scalar confidence score. Subgroup calibration and multicalibration ask whether calibration holds over a specified class of groups or auditors. Slice-discovery methods search for coherent regions of high error or degraded performance that can be measured directly, for example through accuracy or loss. In contrast, we formulate the discovery of signed input-dependent miscalibration as the central problem: given only observed triples (xi,fi,yi)(x_{i},f_{i},y_{i}), recover regions where the conditional residual Y−f⁡(X)Y-f(X) is systematically positive or negative. This defines a miscalibration field over the input space, rather than a scalar calibration curve, a fixed subgroup constraint, or an unsigned error slice. The representation-learning procedure we propose is designed specifically to estimate this field and expose regimes of over- and underconfidence that can cancel under confidence-conditioned diagnostics.

Confidence-based calibration.

Classical calibration studies the relationship between a model’s predicted confidence and its empirical correctness. Early work on probabilistic forecasting formalised calibration as a property of conditional outcome frequencies given predicted probabilities, and reliability diagrams became a standard tool for visualising this relationship [5, 6]. Calibration is commonly evaluated by binning predictions by confidence and comparing average confidence with empirical accuracy, alongside scalar metrics such as expected calibration error (ECE) [8]. A related line of work studies post-hoc recalibration methods that learn a one-dimensional map from model scores to calibrated probabilities, including Platt scaling [22], isotonic regression [29], and temperature scaling [8]. More recent work replaces hard binning with smooth nonparametric estimates in confidence space, leading to smoothed reliability diagrams and SmoothECE [2]. These methods provide effective score-level diagnostics and recalibration, but they do not distinguish examples with identical confidence scores that belong to different calibration regimes.

Slice analysis, subgroup calibration, and multicalibration.

A complementary line of work argues that aggregate calibration can mask systematic failures on subpopulations. In fairness and risk prediction, calibration has been studied across protected groups, revealing both the importance of group-conditional reliability and fundamental tensions between calibration and other fairness criteria [16, 3, 19]. More generally, subgroup calibration and multicalibration require calibration to hold not only globally, but simultaneously over a collection of subpopulations or tests [11, 9]. These frameworks formalise the idea that reliability should be assessed beyond the aggregate population and provide strong guarantees when the relevant subgroup class is specified. However, they typically rely on a predefined family of groups, auditors, or test functions. Our setting is complementary: rather than requiring calibration over a predefined group family or auditor class, we aim to discover the calibration-relevant geometry itself.

Automatic subgroup and error-slice discovery.

Automatic slice-discovery methods aim to find coherent subsets on which a model underperforms. [4] and [23] identify interpretable high-error subpopulations for model validation and debugging. Representation-based approaches extend this idea to higher-dimensional settings; [7], for example, combines cross-modal embeddings with an error-aware mixture model to identify and describe error slices. In NLP and LLM settings, [13] introduce an automatic slice-detection benchmark for NLP, [20] study representation choices for clustering offensive-language errors, and [30] formalise active slice discovery for LLMs with limited slice-membership annotation. Unlike error-slice discovery, which typically targets elevated loss or misclassification rate, our target is signed residual structure: a region may have the same accuracy as another while differing in whether the model is overconfident or underconfident.

Calibration studies of LLMs.

Recent work studies calibration in large language models across several notions of confidence, including token probabilities, multiple-choice answer probabilities, verbalised confidence, and semantic uncertainty. [31] provide a systematic study across pretraining and alignment stages, showing that calibration depends strongly on training stage, task format, and alignment procedure. A recurring finding is that pretrained or base models can exhibit meaningful calibration, while fine-tuning, instruction tuning, preference alignment, and chain-of-thought reasoning can degrade it. For example, [10] show that fine-tuned pretrained language models can become overconfident, especially under distribution shift; [27] study calibration degradation after preference alignment and propose calibration-aware fine-tuning methods; and [18] show that base LLMs can be well calibrated over semantic answer classes, while RL instruction tuning and chain-of-thought can break this calibration. Other work develops methods for eliciting or improving LLM confidence estimates, including calibration tuning [15]. Our work is complementary: rather than asking only whether an LLM is globally calibrated, we show that LLM embeddings encode information that can be used to learn input-dependent miscalibration fields, revealing hidden regions of overconfidence and underconfidence missed by aggregate diagnostics.

Broader impact statement.

This work aims to improve model reliability by identifying input regions where confidence is systematically miscalibrated. Such diagnostics can support safer auditing, model debugging, and decisions about when to defer or seek additional validation. However, the method should not be interpreted as a guarantee of safety or correctness. Discovered regimes depend on the available labelled data and may miss failures on underrepresented groups or deployment conditions. If used uncritically, local confidence correction could create a false sense of reliability, especially in high-stakes settings. We therefore view the method as one component of a broader evaluation pipeline, to be used alongside task-specific validation, fairness analysis, and human oversight.

Appendix B Proxy metric for hyperparameter selection.

In practice, the ground-truth miscalibration field δ⁡(x)\delta(x) is unknown, and oracle metrics such as Corr⁡(δ^ϕ​(X),δ⁡(X))\mathrm{Corr}(\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(X),\delta(X)) cannot be used for model selection. Moreover, the training objective in Eq. (4) depends explicitly on the kernel bandwidth σ\sigma and the representation ϕ\phi, and is therefore not directly comparable across different hyperparameter settings. In particular, a lower validation loss does not necessarily imply better recovery of the miscalibration field. We therefore introduce a proxy criterion for hyperparameter selection that relies only on observable quantities (xi,fi,yi)(x_{i},f_{i},y_{i}) and the estimated local correction δ^ϕ​(x)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x).

The key idea is to interpret δ^ϕ​(x)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) as a local probability correction to the base confidence f⁡(x)f(x). For a given input, we define the corrected prediction

f~raw​(x):=f⁡(x)+δ^ϕ​(x).\tilde{f}_{\text{raw}}(x):=f(x)+\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x).

We evaluate the quality of this correction on a validation set using the Brier score

BS⁡(p,y):=(y−p)2.\mathrm{BS}(p,y):=(y-p)^{2}.

Compared to log-loss, the Brier score is less sensitive to extreme predictions near 00 and 11, making it more stable when evaluating local corrections.

We define the proxy metric as the corrected validation Brier score

Proxy⁡(σ,ϕ):=1n​∑i=1n(yi−f~raw​(xi))2.\mathrm{Proxy}(\sigma,\phi):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(y_{i}-\tilde{f}_{\text{raw}}(x_{i})\Big)^{2}. (6)

Lower values of Proxy⁡(σ,ϕ)\mathrm{Proxy}(\sigma,\phi) indicate that the learned local correction improves predictive accuracy.

This quantity depends only on (fi,yi)(f_{i},y_{i}) and δ^ϕ​(xi)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x_{i}), and can therefore be computed without access to δ⁡(x)\delta(x) or η⁡(x)\eta(x).

The proxy admits a natural statistical interpretation. The Brier score is a strictly proper scoring rule, so in expectation it is minimised by the true conditional probability η⁡(x)\eta(x). Consequently, if δ^ϕ​(x)\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x) is aligned with the true miscalibration field, the corrected predictor f~​(x)\tilde{f}(x) will improve validation Brier score. Minimizing Proxy⁡(σ,ϕ)\mathrm{Proxy}(\sigma,\phi) therefore favours hyperparameters that yield locally informative and well-aligned estimates of the miscalibration field.

Var⁡(δ^ϕ​(x)∣{xi}i=1n,ϕ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)\mid\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},\phi\right) =Var(∑i=1nwi(x)ri|{xi}i=1n,ϕ)\displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}(x)r_{i}\,\middle|\,\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},\phi\right)
=∑i=1nwi​(x)2​Var​(ri∣xi)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}(x)^{2}\mathrm{Var}(r_{i}\mid x_{i})
≤C0​∑i=1nwi​(x)2.\displaystyle\leq C_{0}\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}(x)^{2}.

If the kernel is bounded as 0≤K⁡(⋅,⋅)≤Kmax0\leq K(\cdot,\cdot)\leq K_{\max}, then

∑i=1nwi​(x)2=∑i=1nK​(ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(xi))2m​(x)2≤Kmax​∑i=1nK⁡(ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(xi))m​(x)2=Kmaxm⁡(x).\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}(x)^{2}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K(\phi(x),\phi(x_{i}))^{2}}{m(x)^{2}}\leq\frac{K_{\max}\sum_{i=1}^{n}K(\phi(x),\phi(x_{i}))}{m(x)^{2}}=\frac{K_{\max}}{m(x)}.

Therefore,

Var⁡(δ^ϕ​(x)∣{xi}i=1n,ϕ)≤C0​Kmaxm⁡(x).\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)\mid\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},\phi\right)\leq\frac{C_{0}K_{\max}}{m(x)}.

Setting C=C0​KmaxC=C_{0}K_{\max} proves the claim.

Remark.

The bound treats ϕ\phi as fixed, isolating the variance-reduction effect of kernel averaging in a chosen geometry. It shows that the estimator variance decreases inversely with the effective neighbourhood mass m⁡(x)m(x). In contrast, individual residuals have variance Var⁡(ri∣xi)=η⁡(xi)​(1−η⁡(xi))=𝒪⁡(1)\mathrm{Var}(r_{i}\mid x_{i})=\eta(x_{i})(1-\eta(x_{i}))=\mathcal{O}(1), which does not diminish with sample size in the absence of repeated observations at the same input. In the full algorithm, ϕ\phi is learned from residuals, so the neighbourhood-mass regulariser in Eq. (4) and validation-based model selection are needed to avoid degenerate geometries with m⁡(x)≈1m(x)\approx 1 that fit pointwise Bernoulli noise.

This result is therefore not a recovery guarantee for the learned geometry. We include it to clarify the statistical role of kernel averaging and neighbourhood mass, rather than as a main theoretical contribution. The question of when the learned representation recovers the true calibration geometry remains an open theoretical problem.

Appendix D Implementation Details

D.1 Representation learning network

The network ϕ\phi is a feedforward MLP with LL hidden layers of width hh, GELU activations, and an output projection of dimension doutd_{\text{out}} followed by ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalisation. Its capacity differs between the synthetic and real-data settings to reflect the input dimensionality:

  • •

    Synthetic experiments. The input is a 2-dimensional embedding (din=2d_{\text{in}}=2). We use h=256h=256, L=2L=2, dout=64d_{\text{out}}=64.

  • •

    LLM experiments. The input is the final-layer last-token hidden state of the frozen base model (dmodeld_{\text{model}}). We use h=512h=512, L=2L=2, dout=128d_{\text{out}}=128. dmodeld_{\text{model}} varies by model family and size.

A dropout rate of 0.10.1 is applied between hidden layers.

D.2 Training objective

We minimise the kernel-discovery loss

ℒ(ϕ)=−1n∑i=1nδ^ϕ(xi)2+λ1n∑i=1n[max(0,mmin−mi)]2,\mathcal{L}(\phi)=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x_{i})^{2}+\lambda\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\max(0,m_{\min}-m_{i})\right]^{2},

where

δ^ϕ​(x)=∑i=1nKσ​(ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(xi))​ri∑i=1nKσ​(ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(xi)),mi:=∑j=1nKσ​(ϕ⁡(xi),ϕ⁡(xj))\widehat{\delta}_{\phi}(x)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{\sigma}(\phi(x),\phi(x_{i}))\,r_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{\sigma}(\phi(x),\phi(x_{i}))},\quad m_{i}:=\sum_{j=1}^{n}K_{\sigma}(\phi(x_{i}),\phi(x_{j}))

using the Gaussian kernel:

Kσ​(ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(x′))=exp⁡(−‖ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(x′)‖2σ2).K_{\sigma}(\phi(x),\phi(x^{\prime}))=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\phi(x)-\phi(x^{\prime})\|^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right).

We set mmin=20m_{\text{min}}=20 and optimise the penalty strength λ\lambda and the kernel bandwidth σ\sigma via hyperparameter tuning. Checkpoint selection and hyperparameter tuning use the corrected validation Brier score computed on the validation split, as described in E.5.

D.3 Optimisation

All models are trained with Adam (lr=×10−5\text{lr}=3\!\times\!10^{-5}, weight decay ×10−67\!\times\!10^{-6}), batch size 10241024, gradient-norm clipping at 1.01.0, and a maximum of 100100 epochs. We use early stopping with patience 2020, and restore the best checkpoint by the validation metric. Training runs on a single A100 NVIDIA GPU.

D.4 Computational Cost and Scalability

The main computational cost of the method comes from evaluating kernel neighbourhoods. Given a query set of size nevaln_{\mathrm{eval}} and a training neighbour bank of size nbankn_{\mathrm{bank}}, exact smoothing against the bank has time complexity O⁡(neval​nbank​dout)O(n_{\mathrm{eval}}n_{\mathrm{bank}}d_{\mathrm{out}}), where doutd_{\mathrm{out}} is the dimension of the learned representation ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x). In our experiments, the neighbour bank is a uniformly sampled subset of the training split capped at nbank=20,000n_{\mathrm{bank}}=20{,}000 examples. Thus, the evaluation cost scales linearly with the evaluation set size and with the capped bank size.

In our implementation, smoothing is exact with respect to the sampled bank but chunked over query points. For a query chunk of size QQ, we compute the Q×nbankQ\times n_{\mathrm{bank}} distance matrix, apply the Gaussian kernel, and multiply by the bank residuals. Thus, the peak memory cost is O⁡(Q​nbank)O(Qn_{\mathrm{bank}}) rather than O⁡(neval​nbank)O(n_{\mathrm{eval}}n_{\mathrm{bank}}), and the full query-by-bank kernel matrix is never materialized.

During representation learning, the quadratic kernel computation is performed within minibatches rather than over the full training set. For minibatch size BB, computing all pairwise representation-space kernels costs O⁡(B2​dout)O(B^{2}d_{\mathrm{out}}) time and O⁡(B2)O(B^{2}) memory. The quadratic cost is controlled by the minibatch size, while validation and test evaluation use the capped training neighbour bank.

All experiments in this paper use exact kernel evaluations with respect to a uniformly sampled training bank capped at 20,00020{,}000 examples. We choose this simple bank-sampling strategy because it preserves the training distribution in expectation and fixes the maximum cost of evaluation at O⁡(neval⋅20,000⋅dout)O(n_{\mathrm{eval}}\cdot 20{,}000\cdot d_{\mathrm{out}}). The resulting estimator can be viewed as a Monte Carlo approximation to full-bank smoothing. Alternative scaling strategies include restricting the kernel average to the top-kk nearest neighbours in the learned representation [24, 14].

As a representative synchronized runtime on a single A100 GPU, for a setting with ntest=9,103n_{\mathrm{test}}=9{,}103, ntrain≈70​kn_{\mathrm{train}}\approx 70\mathrm{k}, nbank=20,000n_{\mathrm{bank}}=20{,}000, and dout=128d_{\mathrm{out}}=128, training the representation map ϕ\phi took approximately 4040 minutes. Computing ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) for the test split took 4.74.7 seconds, building the sampled neighbour bank took 10.210.2 seconds, and computing test-set field values by exact kernel averaging against the sampled bank took 0.010.01 seconds.

D.5 Datasets

Synthetic data.

Construction of the synthetic datasets is described in Appendix E.1.

Real data.

For the real-data experiments we use four real-world datasets: HH-RLHF, MedMCQA, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, each scored under one of twelve base model checkpoints from Hugging Face: Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Qwen3-4B-Base, Qwen3-8B-Base, Ministral-3-3B-Base-2512, Ministral-3-8B-Base-2512, Ministral-3-14B-Base-2512, Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, gemma-3-1b-pt, gemma-3-4b-pt, gemma-3-12b-pt. For each model–dataset pair we precompute (i) the last-token hidden state of the base model on the prompt, and (ii) the model’s predicted confidence f⁡(x)f(x).

For HH-RLHF, confidence values indicate the model-assigned probability that the first of two candidate responses is preferred. The label yy is therefore y=1y=1 if the ground-truth human preference label indicates the first response and y=0y=0 otherwise. For the remaining multiple-choice datasets, we define the binary variable as the correctness of the model’s selected answer: y=1y=1 if the answer with highest model probability is correct and y=0y=0 otherwise. The associated confidence score f⁡(x)f(x) is the model probability assigned to this selected answer. Sample sizes range from ≈12​k\approx 12\text{k} (MMLU-Pro) to ≈193​k\approx 193\text{k} (MedMCQA). All datasets are split 80/10/1080/10/10 into train/validation/test by a random permutation.

Prompt formats for eliciting LLM confidence scores.

To elicit the LLM confidence scores we use the prompt formats presented in Prompt 1 and 2. We treat LLMs as black-box probabilistic classifiers whose output is a distribution over a fixed set of candidate completions 𝒱\mathcal{V} (the answer letters). For each candidate v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V} we compute the conditional log-likelihood log⁡pLLM​(v∣prompt)\log p_{\text{LLM}}(v\mid\text{prompt}) as the sum of the token-level log-probabilities of vv and normalize across candidates with a softmax:

p~​(v∣prompt)=exp⁡(log⁡pLLM​(v∣prompt))∑v′∈𝒱exp⁡(log⁡pLLM​(v′∣prompt)).\tilde{p}(v\mid\text{prompt})\;=\;\frac{\exp\bigl(\log p_{\text{LLM}}(v\mid\text{prompt})\bigr)}{\sum_{v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}}\exp\bigl(\log p_{\text{LLM}}(v^{\prime}\mid\text{prompt})\bigr)}.

This restriction to 𝒱\mathcal{V} removes probability mass that the LLM would otherwise assign to off-task tokens (whitespace, alternative phrasings of the answer, etc.) and yields a well-defined Bernoulli / categorical predictive distribution that we can study.

MMLU, MMLU-Pro, MedMCQA. For these multi-choice datasets we use Prompt 1. The candidate set is the set of answer letters 𝒱={A,B,C,…}\mathcal{V}=\{\text{A},\text{B},\text{C},\dots\} (|𝒱|=4|\mathcal{V}|=4 for MedMCQA, between 44 and 1010 for MMLU and MMLU-Pro). The base predictor is the LLM’s confidence in its top choice,

f⁡(x)=maxv∈𝒱⁡p~​(v∣prompt​(x)),f(x)\;=\;\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\tilde{p}(v\mid\text{prompt}(x)),

and the binary outcome is the correctness indicator

y= 1[argmaxv∈𝒱p~(v∣prompt(x))=v⋆(x)],y\;=\;\mathbbm{1}\bigl[\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\tilde{p}(v\mid\text{prompt}(x))\;=\;v^{\star}(x)\bigr],

where v⋆​(x)v^{\star}(x) is the gold answer letter. Calibration is therefore assessed on the LLM’s top-1 confidence.

HH-RLHF (preference judging). We re-purpose the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset as a binary preference-judging task. For each example we extract the user prompt and the chosen / rejected response pair, then assign them to slots A and B uniformly at random; the binary label y=𝟙​[option A is the chosen response]y=\mathbbm{1}[\text{option A is the chosen response}]. We then prompt the LLM with Prompt 2 so that the next token must be either “A” or “B”. The candidate set is 𝒱={A,B}\mathcal{V}=\{\text{A},\text{B}\} and we take

f​(x)=p~​(A∣prompt​(x))f(x)\;=\;\tilde{p}(\text{A}\mid\text{prompt}(x))

as the base predictor, paired directly with yy. A well-calibrated judge should satisfy ℙ⁡[y=1∣f⁡(x)=f]=f\mathbb{P}[y=1\mid f(x)=f]=f across the full [0,1][0,1] range.

Since candidate completions are single tokens, in both cases the sequence of token log-probabilities is computed via a single forward pass per candidate completion (no decoding). Prompt embeddings xx used for the calibration network ϕ\phi are extracted from this same forward pass as the last hidden state at the last input token.

D.6 Diagnositc controls for Recalibration

We compare δ^ϕ\hat{\delta}_{\phi}-based correction to two standard post-hoc calibrators:

  • •

    Temperature scaling. A single scalar TT is fit by full-batch L-BFGS optimisation with respect to the binary negative log likelihood.

  • •

    Isotonic regression. We use the off-the-shelf implementation from scikit-learn.

Both methods are fit on the training splits of datasets.
